elysia-papillosa.klepto_lede: Two individuals from Tampa, Florida, were sequenced with PacBio HiFi reads in 2024: the one used for the assembly and a second animal. The plastid DNA among the reads of each identifies the alga on which it had fed.
klepto_answer: The kleptoplasts came from a single alga, Penicillus lamourouxii (a shaving-brush alga). All {cp_reads} plastid reads from the assembled individual match one plastid genome, with a median identity of {donor1_id}. This genome, OZ494339.1, was assembled by the Sanger Institute from the same individual and deposited as P. lamourouxii. The barcode gene rbcL is present as a single sequence, and so is tufA, apart from 21 of 366 reads in which a run of eight adenines is one base shorter, a common type of sequencing error in homopolymers. There is no evidence of a second alga.

The second individual contained the same alga, but much less plastid DNA. It has {papi1_cp_reads} plastid reads, compared with {cp_reads} in the assembled individual, and plastid DNA makes up {papi1_cp_pct} of the sequenced bases, compared with {cp_pct}. Its rbcL and tufA sequences are identical to those of the first individual. In addition, 17 of its reads are plastid DNA of a flowering plant, 86 to 96% identical to the plastid genome of Arabidopsis; these may derive from seagrass ingested with its food.

The amount of plastid DNA is small. In the assembled individual, plastid DNA makes up {cp_pct} of the sequenced bases, which corresponds to about {depth_ratio} copies of the plastid genome per copy of the slug nuclear genome. By comparison, the E. crispata individual had about 250.
klepto_which: Each read was assigned to the plastid reference that it matches best, and the sequences of the two barcode genes were extracted from every read that spans them.
klepto_nuclei: Almost no algal nuclear DNA is present. Only {rdna_reads} of the {reads} reads from the assembled individual contains nuclear ribosomal DNA of a Penicillus species, and none of the reads from the second individual does. This read is about 99% identical to a P. pyriformis record across the variable spacer regions, where the slug’s own ribosomal DNA does not match at all. A trace of algal nuclear DNA was therefore present in the sample, most likely from food remaining in the gut. No read matches an algal mitochondrial genome.

This is relevant to the question of gene transfer. Because algal nuclear DNA is present, even in trace amounts, an algal gene found among the reads would not in itself show that the gene is part of the slug genome.
klepto_caveats: The identification as P. lamourouxii is based on a single 562-base rbcL record in GenBank (DQ469333), to which the reads are identical, and on the name under which the Sanger Institute deposited the plastid genome. No tufA record is available for the species. The most similar species with full-length barcode sequences, P. dumetosus, is {rbcL_id} (rbcL) and {tufA_id} (tufA) identical.
Both individuals are from the same locality. E. papillosa may also feed on other algae.
All three long-read runs of the project were analysed: {bases} from the assembled individual and {papi1_bases} from the second individual.
elysia-papillosa.transfer_lede: Algal DNA was searched for in the assembly and in the reads. For this species, reads are publicly available from two individuals: the one used for the assembly and a second animal.
transfer_answer: There is no evidence of algal DNA in the genome. No sequence in the assembly joins algal DNA to slug nuclear DNA, and in the reads from two individuals no molecule contains chloroplast DNA flanked on both sides by nuclear DNA.

Assembly. The assembly contains no plastid DNA. One contig of 31 kb is a fragment of a green-algal mitochondrial genome, most likely from the alga in the gut of the animal. It is a separate contig and carries no slug gene.

Reads. In the assembled individual, {join_cp_any} of {join_cp_of} chloroplast reads and {join_mt_any} of {join_mt_of} reads of the slug’s own mitochondrial DNA are joined to nuclear DNA at one end; in the second individual, the numbers are {papi1_join_cp_any} of {papi1_join_cp_of} and {papi1_join_mt_any} of {papi1_join_mt_of}. Chloroplast DNA is thus joined to nuclear DNA no more frequently than mitochondrial DNA is. At a frequency of {per_cell} in the first individual, or {papi1_per_cell} in the second, about three reads with an insertion-like structure would have been expected. None was found.
transfer_assembly: No sequence in the assembly consists of plastid DNA, in whole or in part. The only match retained is a 425 bp region that resembles a mitochondrial ribosomal RNA gene of the green alga Caulerpa. It lies on the contig that the protein search (below) identifies as algal mitochondrial DNA.

loci_readings.CDRNNR020002991.1:19089: A mitochondrial ribosomal RNA gene on a contig of algal mitochondrial DNA (see the protein search).

reads_main: Both long-read runs from the assembled individual were analysed in full. The library was not amplified.

Reads with a single junction. Of the {join_cp_of} chloroplast reads, {join_cp_any} are joined to nuclear DNA at one end ({join_cp} of them to nuclear DNA that maps to a unique position), as are {join_mt_any} of the {join_mt_of} reads of the slug’s own mitochondrial DNA. Each of these reads consists of only two segments, with the organelle segment extending to the end of the read. Mitochondrial DNA is joined to nuclear DNA at least as frequently as chloroplast DNA is. This is expected for chimeras formed during library preparation, but not for insertions of chloroplast DNA. All of these reads are listed in the junction table available for download.

The comparison with nuclear DNA is not informative for this library. Nuclear segments are joined to nuclear DNA from another locus much more frequently ({bg_rate}), but nearly all of these cases reflect real differences between the chromosomes of this individual and an assembly that is still at the contig level.

Reads with an insertion-like structure. None was found, for either chloroplast or mitochondrial DNA. The search included inserts as short as 100 bases within a read that is otherwise collinear with the nuclear sequence.
transfer_proteins: The only locus for which the best match is an algal protein lies on contig CDRNNR020002991.1 (30.9 kb). When translated in all six reading frames, this contig carries a series of mitochondrial genes (nad5, cox2, nad3, atpA and nad4) whose best matches are mitochondrial proteins of green algae, and atpA is interrupted by introns. The contig is a fragment of an algal mitochondrial genome that was assembled separately, and it should be excluded when the assembly is used as slug sequence.

protein_readings.CDRNNR020002991.1: A fragment of a green-algal mitochondrial genome, with a series of mitochondrial genes and no slug gene.

transfer_caveats: The detection limits given here are averages over all the cells that contributed DNA to the library. Kleptoplasts are present only in cells of the digestive gland. If these made up one tenth of the cells of the animal, the limit for these cells alone would be ten times weaker.

The analysis of the reads detects plastid DNA from the alga present in these animals and from the other algae in the panel. The protein search detects only genes that have a homologue among the 471 query proteins.
The assembly is still at the contig level, and sequence that is missing from it could not be searched.
klepto_rhythm: For animals with the same diet, kleptoplast transcripts should be mapped to OZ494339.1, the plastid genome assembled from the same individual (89,758 bp). This genome is not annotated in the archive. It is 99.4% identical, over nearly its whole length, to OZ372796.1, the second plastid genome from the E. crispata individual, for which gene coordinates derived by homology are available in the downloads for that species.

The algal source of the kleptoplasts changes with the diet of an animal. A transcriptome study should therefore confirm the identity of the kleptoplasts in its own animals, for which the two barcode genes are sufficient.
reads_papi1: The second individual, a whole adult from the same locality, was sequenced to greater depth from a library that had been amplified by PCR. It contained about one tenth as much chloroplast DNA as the first ({papi1_cp_pct} of the bases). Its reads were aligned to the assembly of the first individual.

Reads with a single junction. Of the {papi1_join_cp_of} chloroplast reads, {papi1_join_cp_any} are joined to nuclear DNA at one end, as are {papi1_join_mt_any} of the {papi1_join_mt_of} mitochondrial reads. The amplification adapter lies between the two segments in all {papi1_cp_joins} chloroplast junctions and in {papi1_mt_adapter} of the {papi1_mt_joins} mitochondrial junctions, which shows that these chimeras formed during library preparation.

Reads with an insertion-like structure. None was found. However, {papi1_unconfirmed} reads contain an additional segment that the first pass had matched to a plastid genome on the basis of a few seeds; 28 of these reads are from the same locus. Base-level alignment shows that the segment is not plastid DNA. At this locus the second individual has three more copies of a 45-base repeat than the assembled individual, and the repeat shares a single seed with a repeat in the plastid genome of an unrelated alga.

elysia-atroviridis.klepto_lede: The individual sequenced for the genome was an adult collected at Qingdao, China, in 2024. The plastid DNA among its reads identifies the alga on which it had fed.
klepto_answer: The kleptoplasts came from Bryopsis (a feather alga). A total of {cp_reads} reads are plastid DNA, and {donor1_pct} of this DNA matches a single plastid genome with a median identity of {donor1_id}. This genome, PQ652170.1, is from China and was deposited as Bryopsis hypnoides.

Two closely related plastid types are present. Each barcode gene occurs as two sequences that differ by about 0.5%. One is found in about 94% of the reads and is identical to PQ652170.1. The other, found in about 6% of the reads, has a tufA sequence identical to GenBank records deposited as B. hypnoides and as B. plumosa. These genes do not clearly separate the species of this group, so the two types are best interpreted as two strains or sister species of Bryopsis.

The plastid content is high. Plastid DNA makes up {cp_pct} of all sequenced bases, which corresponds to about {depth_ratio} copies of the plastid genome per copy of the slug nuclear genome. E. atroviridis is reported to retain functional chloroplasts for only a few days (Cruz et al. 2015), so this animal had probably fed shortly before it was sequenced.
klepto_which: Each read was assigned to the plastid reference that it matches best, and the sequences of the two barcode genes were extracted from every read that spans them.
klepto_nuclei: No read matches algal nuclear ribosomal DNA across the variable spacer regions. In addition, only {algmt_reads} reads match an algal mitochondrial genome, which corresponds to about one base of algal mitochondrial DNA per {cp_per_algmt} bases of plastid DNA. As in E. crispata, the plastids had been retained but almost no other algal DNA.
klepto_caveats: Bryopsis species are difficult to distinguish with rbcL and tufA, and GenBank contains records under several species names that are identical in these genes. The match to PQ652170.1 is exact, but the species name of that record is the one assigned by its submitters.
The results describe a single animal on the day it was collected.
The complete long-read run used for the assembly was analysed ({bases}).
elysia-atroviridis.transfer_lede: Algal DNA was searched for in the assembly and in the reads from which it was built.
transfer_answer: There is no evidence of algal DNA in the genome, and this is the most informative data set on this site. The assembly contains no algal sequence, and none of the {join_cp_of} chloroplast reads contains chloroplast DNA flanked on both sides by nuclear DNA.
Assembly. The assembly contains no plastid DNA, and the protein search found no algal or bacterial gene.

Reads. A total of {join_cp_any} chloroplast reads, or two in every 10,000, are joined to nuclear DNA at one end. Each is a single molecule, as expected for an insertion in a single cell, but each consists of only two segments, as expected for two fragments joined during library preparation. No read has an insertion-like structure. At a frequency of {per_cell}, about three such reads would have been expected.
transfer_assembly: No sequence in the assembly consists of plastid DNA, in whole or in part. The only match retained is a 214 bp region on chromosome 6 that is 85% identical to a transfer RNA gene of a plastid genome.
reads_main: This is the most informative data set among the species analysed here: PacBio HiFi reads from an unamplified library, from the same individual as the assembly, in which {cp_pct} of the DNA is chloroplast DNA.

Reads with a single junction. Of the {join_cp_of} chloroplast reads, {join_cp_any} are joined to nuclear DNA at one end, {join_cp} of them to nuclear DNA that maps to a unique position. Each is a single molecule at a different locus, and all are listed in the junction table available for download. Every one of these reads consists of only two segments: a segment of nuclear DNA, and between 500 bases and 11 kb of chloroplast DNA that extends to the end of the read. Such a read shows only one side of a junction, so the read alone cannot show whether the junction was present in a cell or formed during library preparation.

Two observations can be made. First, these reads are rare: at the same frequency, the {slugmt_n} reads of the slug’s own mitochondrial DNA would be expected to include less than one chimeric read, and none was found. Second, none of them includes a second junction. An insertion shorter than the reads, which average 8.7 kb in this library, would usually be sequenced in full, as nuclear DNA followed by chloroplast DNA and then by nuclear DNA again. If these {join_cp_any} reads represent insertions, the inserted fragments must be longer than the reads. Two fragments joined end to end during library preparation would give exactly this result.

The comparison with nuclear DNA is not informative for this library. Nuclear segments are joined to nuclear DNA from another locus a hundred times more frequently ({bg_rate}), but nearly all of these cases reflect real differences between the chromosomes of this individual and the assembly, not chimeras formed during library preparation.
Reads with an insertion-like structure. None was found. The search included inserts as short as 100 bases within a read that is otherwise collinear with the nuclear sequence.
transfer_proteins: No locus in this assembly has an algal or bacterial protein as its best match.
transfer_caveats: The detection limits given here are averages over all the cells that contributed DNA to the library. Kleptoplasts are present only in cells of the digestive gland. If these made up one tenth of the cells of the animal, the limit for these cells alone would be ten times weaker.

The analysis of the reads detects plastid DNA from the alga present in this animal and from the other algae in the panel. An insertion of DNA from a different alga would be detected only by the searches of the assembly.
The protein search detects only genes that have a homologue among the 471 query proteins.
Sequence that is missing from the assembly could not be searched, and a fragment of chloroplast DNA inserted in a repeat of the slug genome could not be assigned to a position.
klepto_rhythm: Kleptoplast transcripts should be mapped to PQ652170.1 (Bryopsis hypnoides, 139,745 bp, annotated in GenBank). The main plastid type in this animal is identical to this genome in both barcode genes, and the minor type differs from it by about 0.5%.

E. atroviridis is reported to retain functional chloroplasts for only a few days, so the plastids in an animal derive from its most recent meals, and a rhythm observed in them may be a rhythm of recently ingested algal material.

elysia-marginata.klepto_lede: The genome was assembled from a single individual collected at Kagoshima, Japan, in 2013. The plastid DNA among its reads identifies the alga on which it had fed.
klepto_answer: The kleptoplasts came from Bryopsis (a feather alga). Of the plastid DNA, {donor1_pct} matches a single plastid genome with a median identity of {donor1_id}. This genome, PQ652170.1, is from China and was deposited as Bryopsis hypnoides.

The plastid type is the same as in the E. atroviridis individual. Both barcode genes, extracted from plastid contigs assembled from these reads, are identical to that plastid genome and to the main plastid type in the E. atroviridis individual from Qingdao (over 743 bases of rbcL and 1,228 bases of tufA).
The plastid content is moderate. Plastid DNA makes up {cp_pct} of the sequenced bases, which corresponds to about {depth_ratio} copies of the plastid genome per copy of the slug nuclear genome.
klepto_which: Because these are short reads, a single read cannot span a barcode gene. Each read pair was therefore assigned to the plastid reference that it matches best, and the plastid read pairs were assembled into contigs ({contigs} contigs with a total length of {contig_kb} kb, the longest being {contig_longest_kb} kb), from which the barcode genes were extracted.
klepto_nuclei: Algal mitochondrial DNA is present. A total of {algmt_reads} read pairs match the mitochondrial genome of Bryopsis hypnoides with 99.8% identity, which corresponds to about one base of algal mitochondrial DNA per {cp_per_algmt} bases of plastid DNA.

Short reads cannot show whether algal nuclear DNA is present. The read pairs that match algal ribosomal DNA records do so only in the most conserved regions of the genes, and they match unrelated green algae such as Ulva equally well. These reads derive from the slug’s own ribosomal DNA.
klepto_caveats: Bryopsis species are difficult to distinguish with rbcL and tufA. The match to PQ652170.1 is exact, but the species name of that record is the one assigned by its submitters.
Both short-insert libraries used for the assembly were analysed in full ({bases}).
The reads are deposited in the archive under the name Elysia ornata.
elysia-marginata.transfer_lede: Algal DNA was searched for in the assembly and in the short reads from which it was built.
transfer_answer: There is no evidence of algal DNA in the genome, and this library gives the lowest upper limit obtained from short reads on this site. No sequence in the assembly joins algal DNA to slug nuclear DNA. Among the reads, one chloroplast pair in ten thousand has its mate in nuclear DNA: {cp_chim} pairs in the whole library, each a single molecule at a different locus. One insertion per cell, at a different locus in each cell, would by itself add about that number of pairs. The cells of this animal therefore contained at most about one insertion each, even if every one of these pairs derived from an insertion.

One small sequence in the assembly is plastid DNA. BMAT01005342.1 (3.7 kb) is a region of the Bryopsis plastid genome that is absent from the reference genomes. Read pairs link both of its ends to adjacent regions of the plastid genome, and its read depth is the same as that of the plastid genome. It is kleptoplast DNA, not slug DNA.

About {bact_mb} Mb of the assembly is bacterial. The protein search identified {bact_n} sequences that consist of bacterial DNA along their whole length, from at least three groups of bacteria. The gene set published with the assembly includes genes on these sequences. None of them is algal.
transfer_assembly: The DNA-level search found no plastid sequence in the assembly. The two weak matches retained are ribosomal RNA genes of bacterial type: a 5 kb ribosomal RNA operon and a 1.1 kb region of a large-subunit rRNA gene, the latter on one of the bacterial sequences described below. They match plastid and algal mitochondrial genomes with 80% identity only because the organelle genes are of bacterial origin.

loci_readings.BMAT01004790.1:296870: A large-subunit ribosomal RNA gene of bacterial type.
loci_readings.BMAT01007826.1:4633: A ribosomal RNA operon of bacterial type, 5 kb.

reads_main: Both paired-end libraries were analysed in full. Of the {cp_n} chloroplast pairs, {cp_chim} have their mate in nuclear DNA ({cp_rate}). Of the {slugmt_n} mitochondrial pairs, only one does, which is too few for a comparison of the two organelles. In a random sample of the library, {bg_rate} of nuclear pairs have their two reads on unrelated sequences, in most cases at the ends of assembly sequences. In a further {split_cp} molecules, a single read extends from chloroplast DNA into nuclear DNA ({split_cp_rate} of chloroplast pairs, compared with {bg_split_rate} of nuclear pairs in which a read extends into an unrelated nuclear segment); five of these {split_cp} are the reads at the bacterial sequence listed above.

Upper limit on the number of insertions. In this library, chloroplast DNA is joined to nuclear DNA ten to a hundred times less frequently than in the other short-read libraries on this site, and the library covers the slug genome {slug_depth} times. It is therefore the only short-read library in which the count itself provides an upper limit: the number of discordant pairs and split reads is about the number that one insertion per cell would add (see the values above). Averaged over all the cells that contributed DNA to the library, this animal contained at most about one insertion per cell, and fewer if some of these junctions formed during library preparation, as is the case in every library.

The small plastid sequence. BMAT01005342.1 (3.7 kb) matches no plastid reference, but the read pairs show its origin. One read lies at its start in 225 pairs and at its end in 948 pairs; the mates of these reads map to two positions 4 kb apart in the reference plastid genome, and reads extend beyond the end of the sequence into the adjacent plastid sequence. Its read depth is about 1,500×, the same as that of the plastid genome, compared with {slug_depth}× for nuclear DNA. It is therefore a region of the plastid genome of this alga that is absent from the references and was retained in the assembly, and its read pairs are counted as plastid DNA in the values above.
Each of these pairs and split reads is a single molecule at a different locus. They are listed in the junction table. A genuine junction that was sequenced only once would look the same.
transfer_proteins: The {prot_microbe} loci of bacterial type lie on 24 sequences. When these sequences were translated in full, {bact_n} of them proved to be bacterial along their whole length, with {bact_genes} protein-coding regions of bacterial type that occupy between a quarter and nearly all of each sequence.

These sequences derive from at least three groups of bacteria. Six sequences (735 kb in total, 27 to 29% G+C) are most similar to mycoplasmas. In these sequences the codon TGA, a stop codon in the standard genetic code, occurs within genes about nine times per thousand codons; mycoplasmas translate it as tryptophan. This explains why six of the nine loci first found on BMAT01003247.1 appeared to be interrupted by stop codons. Eleven sequences (1.2 Mb, 36 to 39% G+C) are most similar to flavobacteria and related groups. The other seven are small (4 to 18 kb, 45 to 54% G+C), and most are similar to Pseudomonas and related bacteria. The matches are distant, mostly with 40 to 50% protein identity, so the bacteria are relatives of these groups and not known species.

Of the {prot_microbe} loci, {bact_listed} are included in the gene set published with the assembly, in which these bacterial genes are annotated as slug genes. They will therefore be found in any search of that gene set for genes shared with bacteria or algae. The sequences derive from bacteria that lived in or on the animal and were assembled together with its genome. None of the loci has an algal protein as its best match.
transfer_caveats: Short reads cannot show whether a junction is part of an insertion, so a single pair that joins chloroplast DNA to nuclear DNA cannot be distinguished from a chimera formed during library preparation. The upper limit given above treats all such pairs as if they were insertions.
The assembly contains 82 Mb of gaps, and sequence that is missing from it could not be searched.

The protein search detects only genes that have a homologue among the 471 query proteins. The bacterial sequences listed are those in which the search happened to find a match; the assembly may contain others.
klepto_rhythm: Kleptoplast transcripts should be mapped to PQ652170.1 (Bryopsis hypnoides, 139,745 bp, annotated in GenBank), to which the plastid DNA of this animal is identical in both barcode genes. The plastid contigs assembled from its reads ({contigs} contigs, {contig_kb} kb) are available in the downloads; they include a 3.7 kb region that is absent from the reference.
The reads are deposited under the name Elysia ornata. Other individuals of the species may contain kleptoplasts from other Bryopsis species, which can be checked with the two barcode genes.

break_notes.BMAT01004028.1:131228: This position is a gap in one of the bacterial sequences in the assembly (see below). The reads continue into the end of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene of that bacterium, which is missing from the assembly at this position, and 41 bases of this gene are identical to a cyanobacterial genome that is included in the panel to detect distant matches. The sequence is not chloroplast DNA.

elysia-timida.klepto_lede: The genome was assembled from adults collected at Cadaqués, Spain. E. timida is known to feed on Acetabularia acetabulum (mermaid’s wineglass). The reads are consistent with this, as far as the available reference sequences allow.
klepto_answer: The kleptoplasts came from Acetabularia acetabulum. Of the plastid DNA that could be identified, {donor1_pct} matches GenBank records of this alga, with a median identity of {donor1_id}. The remainder matches plastid genes of other algae of the same order with about 90% identity; these are Acetabularia genes for which no A. acetabulum sequence is available in GenBank.

Most of the plastid DNA could not be identified. No complete plastid genome of Acetabularia has been published. GenBank contains 51 fragments with a total length of 49 kb, which is only part of the genome. Only reads that overlap one of these fragments, or a similar gene of a related alga, were counted, so the value of {cp_pct} of sequenced bases is a minimum.

Nevertheless, the plastid content is low. The known fragments of the plastid genome have a read depth of about {cp_depth}×, compared with {nuc_depth}× for the slug nuclear genome. In the E. crispata individual, the read depth of the plastid genome was about 250 times that of the nuclear genome. Part of this difference may be due to the way in which the library was prepared (see below).
klepto_which: Each read was assigned to the plastid reference that it matches best. In the complete run, both barcode genes are spanned by reads: tufA by {tufA_reads} reads, which all have the same sequence and are identical to the A. acetabulum record over 1,230 bases, and rbcL by {rbcL_reads} reads, which all have the same sequence and are {rbcL_id} identical to the A. acetabulum record.
klepto_nuclei: No read matches algal nuclear ribosomal DNA across the variable spacer regions, and none matches an algal mitochondrial genome.
klepto_caveats: For the reason given above, the proportion of plastid DNA is a minimum. A complete Acetabularia plastid genome would be needed to measure it.
The library was amplified by PCR from a very small amount of DNA, which distorts the proportions of the sequenced DNA.
The complete run used for the assembly was analysed ({bases}).
elysia-timida.transfer_lede: Algal DNA was searched for in the assembly and in the reads from which it was built. For this species, the analysis of the reads is limited by the small part of the algal plastid genome that has been sequenced.
transfer_answer: There is no evidence of algal DNA in the genome, within the limits of this library. The assembly contains no algal sequence, and no read contains chloroplast DNA flanked on both sides by nuclear DNA.
Assembly. The assembly contains no plastid DNA, and the protein search found no algal or bacterial gene.

Reads. Of the {join_cp_of} reads that contain chloroplast DNA, {join_cp_any} are joined to nuclear DNA at one end, and {cp_adapter} of these junctions contain the adapter used in the amplification step, which shows that they formed during library preparation. Mitochondrial DNA is joined to nuclear DNA at the same frequency. Because only a small part of the algal plastid genome has been sequenced, most of its DNA could not be identified in the reads.
transfer_assembly: No sequence in the assembly consists of plastid DNA, in whole or in part. Two short regions match algal ribosomal DNA with 94 and 97% identity over about 400 bp. This is the most conserved part of the ribosomal RNA genes, and the regions are most simply explained as the slug’s own ribosomal DNA.

loci_readings.CM092933.1:16209253: The conserved core of a ribosomal RNA gene, most likely the slug’s own.
loci_readings.JBHHFL010000219.1:27010: The conserved core of a ribosomal RNA gene, most likely the slug’s own.

reads_main: The complete run was analysed. The library was amplified by PCR from a very small amount of DNA, a procedure that occasionally joins unrelated molecules.

Reads with a single junction. Of the {join_cp_of} reads that contain chloroplast DNA, {join_cp_any} are joined to nuclear DNA at one end ({cp_rate}), as are {join_mt_any} of the {join_mt_of} reads of the slug’s own mitochondrial DNA ({slugmt_rate}). The two frequencies are the same, as expected for chimeras formed during library preparation. The amplification adapter lies between the two segments in {cp_adapter} of the {cp_joins} chloroplast junctions and in {mt_adapter} of the {mt_joins} mitochondrial junctions, which shows that these junctions formed during amplification.

This leaves {cp_no_adapter} chloroplast junctions without an adapter, each in a single molecule: part of psaB joined to chromosome 2, part of accD joined to chromosome 14, and part of rps14 joined to chromosome 4. They are listed in the junction table. They do not differ in any respect from the {mt_no_adapter} mitochondrial junctions that also lack the adapter, and no difference would be expected, because a genuine junction that is sequenced once from one side looks the same.

Reads with an insertion-like structure. None was found. Three reads contain an additional kilobase of sequence at one locus on chromosome 1 that the first pass matched to a plastid genome, but this sequence is a tandem array of short repeats that resembles a repeat in that plastid genome, and is not chloroplast DNA.
transfer_proteins: No locus in this assembly has an algal or bacterial protein as its best match.
transfer_caveats: Only 49 kb of the Acetabularia plastid genome is available in GenBank. A read that joins nuclear DNA to any other part of that genome would not be detected in the analysis of the reads. The searches of the assembly are not limited in this way for genes, because they use the proteins of other algae as queries.

The detection limits given here are averages over all the cells that contributed DNA to the library. Kleptoplasts are present only in cells of the digestive gland. If these made up one tenth of the cells of the animal, the limit for these cells alone would be ten times weaker.
Sequence that is missing from the assembly could not be searched.
klepto_rhythm: No complete Acetabularia plastid genome is available as a reference for mapping transcripts. GenBank contains 51 fragments of the A. acetabulum plastid genome, with a total length of 49 kb.

A larger set of sequences is available from another source. One assembly of E. crispata (the Purdue assembly, GCA_033675545.1) contains 646 kb of Acetabularia plastid DNA as separate contigs, derived from an animal that had fed on that alga (see the gene-transfer page for E. crispata). These contigs are from a different species of Acetabularia: for the genes that can be compared, they are 90 to 96% identical to those of A. acetabulum. They are therefore useful as a guide to the gene content of the genome, but not as a reference for quantifying reads.
elysia-timida.could_show_main: For this species the value overestimates the sensitivity, because an inserted fragment could be recognised only if it derived from the 49 kb of the plastid genome that have been sequenced.

elysia-leucolegnote.card: Boodleopsis sp. and other algae (in two other individuals)
elysia-leucolegnote.klepto_lede: No reads from the individual used for the assembly are publicly available. Two other individuals of the species, one from Shenzhen and one from Hainan, have been sequenced with short reads, and their plastid DNA was analysed instead.
klepto_answer: The main source of the kleptoplasts in both individuals is a species of Boodleopsis. Of the plastid DNA that could be identified, {donor1_pct} in the Shenzhen individual and {hainan_donor1_pct} in the Hainan individual matches the plastid genome of a Boodleopsis species. Contigs assembled from these reads are 97 to 99% identical to that genome. Boodleopsis, a small green alga that grows on mangrove mud, is the reported food of this slug (Swennen 2011).

The alga is not the Boodleopsis species represented by a barcode sequence in GenBank. The rbcL gene of the main alga is {rbcL_best_id} identical to the B. pusilla record in GenBank. The plastid genome that it matches was deposited as Boodleopsis sp., without a species name. The plastid genomes from the two individuals are 99.5% identical to each other over 71 kb.

Other algae are also present. In the Shenzhen individual, the plastid contigs fall into groups with different read depths (see the table below). The Boodleopsis genome has a read depth of about {cg1_depth}×. {Cg2_n} contigs that do not closely match any reference ({cg2_id} identical to the closest) have a depth of about {cg2_depth}×. They represent a second alga with no close relative in GenBank, about one quarter as abundant as the first. The fragment of plastid DNA found in the assembly (see the gene-transfer page) has a depth of {locus1_depth}× in this individual, similar to the contigs of that alga. A further {cg3_n} contigs are within 5% of another Boodleopsis plastid genome in GenBank, that of isolate FL1161, and have a depth of about {cg3_depth}×; they represent a second Boodleopsis species, present in small amounts.

The other algae are more abundant in the Hainan individual. Its Boodleopsis genome has a read depth of about {hainan_cg1_depth}×. The alga without a reference is also present, with a sequence identical to that in the Shenzhen individual and a depth of 75 to 124×. A third plastid genome, which is 86 to 89% identical to the second in the same genes and no more similar to any reference, has a depth of 150 to 210×, and is thus as abundant as the Boodleopsis genome. In this individual, therefore, two algae that cannot be identified contributed more plastid DNA than the one that can.

Identified plastid DNA makes up {cp_pct} of the sequenced bases in the Shenzhen individual and {hainan_cp_pct} in the Hainan individual. A read is counted as plastid DNA only if it resembles a reference sequence, so algae without a close reference are under-represented in these values and in the proportions given above. Both values are therefore minimum estimates.
klepto_which: Because these are short reads, a single read cannot span a barcode gene. Each read pair was assigned to the plastid reference that it matches best, and the plastid read pairs were assembled into contigs, from which the barcode genes were extracted. The reads from the Shenzhen individual yielded {contigs} contigs (with a total length of {contig_kb} kb, the longest being {contig_longest_kb} kb), and those from the Hainan individual yielded {hainan_contigs} contigs ({hainan_contig_kb} kb).
klepto_nuclei: Short reads cannot show whether algal nuclear DNA is present. The read pairs that match algal ribosomal DNA records do so only in the most conserved regions of the genes, and they match unrelated green algae such as Ulva equally well. These reads derive from the slug’s own ribosomal DNA.
klepto_caveats: Neither individual is the one whose genome was assembled (isolate GZ-2025, Dongzhai Harbor, Hainan). The kleptoplasts of that individual are unknown, apart from the single fragment of plastid DNA in its assembly.
The identification is based on a plastid genome that was deposited without a species name. The match is close but not exact, so the alga may be a different species of the same genus.
The proportions refer to plastid DNA that resembles a reference sequence in the panel. Algae without a close reference are under-represented.
Both libraries were analysed in full: {bases} from the Shenzhen individual and {hainan_bases} from the Hainan individual.
elysia-leucolegnote.transfer_lede: The data for this species are the least informative on this site. No reads from the assembled individual are publicly available, and one third of the bases in the public assembly are masked. The assembly was searched in its public form, and the reads from two other individuals were compared with it.
transfer_answer: There is no evidence of algal DNA in the genome, but the power of the test is low. In two other individuals, read pairs join chloroplast DNA to nuclear DNA about as frequently as they join one nuclear segment to an unrelated one, and somewhat more frequently than they join mitochondrial DNA to nuclear DNA. No such difference is found in the long-read libraries on this site, and the reads that span a junction show that library preparation does not affect the two organelle DNAs in the same way (see below), so the difference cannot be interpreted as evidence of insertions. Short reads could not reveal an insertion that is present in only a few cells.

One small sequence in the assembly begins with plastid genes. JBQKML010000381.1 (9.4 kb, unplaced) starts with 863 bases of plastid DNA, comprising parts of the genes chlL and chlN, and continues as slug nuclear DNA. Both of the other individuals contain the same plastid sequence, at a read depth several times that of nuclear DNA, and in both it continues as plastid DNA beyond base 863: {locus1_right_stop} and {hainan_locus1_right_stop} reads diverge from the assembly at that position, and none spans it. In these individuals the sequence is plastid DNA from an alga on which they had fed. The junction is present only in the assembly, and the individual used for the assembly cannot be tested.
{Bact_n} sequences in the assembly are bacterial, with a total length of {bact_mb} Mb. None of these findings represents algal DNA in the slug genome.
transfer_assembly: Both of the matches retained are examined further below. One is a 416 bp region of the plastid gene chlN near the start of JBQKML010000381.1, which is 87% identical to a Boodleopsis plastid genome. The other is a small-subunit ribosomal RNA gene of bacterial type on JBQKML010000169.1, one of the bacterial sequences.

loci_readings.JBQKML010000381.1:294: The plastid gene chlN, within the first 863 bases of a 9.4 kb unplaced sequence that continues as slug nuclear DNA. Tested with reads (see below).
loci_readings.JBQKML010000169.1:81064: A small-subunit ribosomal RNA gene of bacterial type, on a bacterial sequence.

reads_main: The complete library was analysed. Of the {cp_n} chloroplast pairs, {cp_chim} have their mate in nuclear DNA ({cp_rate}). The corresponding frequency for mitochondrial pairs is {slugmt_rate}, and in a random sample of the library {bg_rate} of nuclear pairs have their two reads on unrelated sequences. In a further {split_cp} molecules, a single read extends from chloroplast DNA into nuclear DNA. This is {split_cp_rate} of chloroplast pairs, compared with {split_mt_rate} for mitochondrial DNA and {bg_split_rate} of nuclear pairs in which a read extends into an unrelated nuclear segment.

Frequencies. Chloroplast DNA is joined to nuclear DNA about as frequently as nuclear DNA is joined to unrelated nuclear DNA, and {cp_mt_ratio} times as frequently as mitochondrial DNA is. The same pattern is found in the Hainan individual. The second E. chlorotica adult shows the same tendency, although it has too few mitochondrial pairs for a firm conclusion, and E. marginata has only one mitochondrial junction. In the long-read libraries on this site there is no such excess: chloroplast DNA is joined to nuclear DNA as frequently as mitochondrial DNA is, and in E. crispata as frequently as bacterial DNA is. Genuine insertions in somatic cells would raise the frequency for chloroplast DNA in exactly this way, so the difference was examined further.

The terminal segment of split reads. A read that spans a junction starts at the end of its fragment, so the segment at the start of the read is the short terminal segment of the fragment, and the other segment extends into the fragment. If a chromosome carrying an insertion is fragmented at random, the organelle segment should be the terminal segment equally often for both organelles: in about {end_mt_expected} of the mitochondrial junctions and {end_cp_expected} of the chloroplast junctions, given the sensitivity of the method. (These values are derived from two controls. First, the first and the last {endpass_piece} bases of a read pass the identity criterion almost equally often; for nuclear DNA the values are {endpass_slug_start} and {endpass_slug_end}. Second, among simulated reads that start with a short segment of organelle DNA and continue as nuclear DNA, the first pass detects {fp_mt} for mitochondrial DNA and {fp_cp} for chloroplast DNA.) If, instead, two fragments were joined end to end during library preparation, the terminal segment is a short fragment, and a type of DNA that is rare among short fragments will seldom be the terminal segment and will be joined less frequently overall.

In the chloroplast junctions of this individual, the terminal segment is chloroplast DNA in {end_cp_org} of {end_cp_n} molecules. In the mitochondrial junctions, it is mitochondrial DNA in {end_mt_org} of {end_mt_n} molecules. In the Hainan individual the values are {hainan_end_cp_org} of {hainan_end_cp_n} and {hainan_end_mt_org} of {hainan_end_mt_n}. The two organelles therefore differ in how often the organelle segment is the terminal one. Random fragmentation cannot produce this difference, but the joining of separate fragments can, if short fragments of mitochondrial DNA were less abundant in the library than short fragments of chloroplast DNA. In that case mitochondrial DNA takes part in fewer chimeras, and its frequency underestimates the rate at which library preparation joins chloroplast DNA to other DNA. The difference between the two organelles cannot therefore be interpreted as evidence of insertions. If it were due to insertions, it would correspond to about {excess_per_cell} insertions per cell in this individual, each at a different locus.

The individual junctions. Many fragments in this library were sequenced twice, and the {cp_chim} pairs derive from {mix_cp_mol} different molecules. The junctions are distributed over the chromosomes in proportion to chromosome length and along the whole plastid genome, each at a different locus, and all are listed in the junction table. None of them can be distinguished from chimeras formed during library preparation, and no difference would be expected, because a genuine junction that is sequenced once looks the same.
reads_hainan: The complete library was analysed. Of the {hainan_cp_n} chloroplast pairs, {hainan_cp_chim} have their mate in nuclear DNA ({hainan_cp_rate}), compared with {hainan_slugmt_rate} of mitochondrial pairs and {hainan_bg_rate} of nuclear pairs in the random sample. A further {hainan_split_cp} reads span a junction ({hainan_split_cp_rate}, compared with {hainan_split_mt_rate} for mitochondrial DNA and {hainan_bg_split_rate} for nuclear DNA).

One tenth of these pairs lie at the ribosomal RNA genes of the bacterial sequence (see above). When they are excluded, chloroplast DNA is joined to nuclear DNA {hainan_cp_mt_ratio} times as frequently as mitochondrial DNA is, a difference similar to that in the Shenzhen individual, and the split reads indicate the same explanation. The terminal segment of the fragment is mitochondrial DNA in {hainan_end_mt_org} of {hainan_end_mt_n} mitochondrial junctions. In the chloroplast junctions it is chloroplast DNA in {hainan_end_cp_org} of {hainan_end_cp_n}, well above the {hainan_end_cp_expected} expected under random fragmentation. Short fragments of chloroplast DNA were thus abundant in this library, which indicates the joining of separate fragments and not insertions. If the whole difference were due to insertions, it would correspond to about {hainan_excess_per_cell} insertions per cell. Apart from the two loci listed, which are the same two as in the Shenzhen individual, no junction is found in two molecules.
transfer_proteins: The loci of bacterial type lie on four unplaced sequences. When translated in full, each of these sequences is bacterial along its whole length, with {bact_genes} protein-coding regions of bacterial type in {bact_mb} Mb, most of which is on JBQKML010000180.1 (1.09 Mb) and JBQKML010000169.1 (747 kb). Their G+C content is 46 to 48%, compared with {genome_gc} for the genome. The most similar proteins are those of well-studied bacteria, with about 40% identity, so this bacterium has no close relative among the reference proteins. It lived in or on the animal and was assembled together with its genome.

The only plastid genes are chlL and chlN at the start of JBQKML010000381.1, with 77% protein identity to those of Udotea. One further locus has an algal protein as its best match by a narrow margin: a ferredoxin reductase gene on the largest bacterial sequence, which is one of the genes of that bacterium.

protein_readings.JBQKML010000381.1: Parts of the plastid genes chlL and chlN in the first 863 bases, followed by slug nuclear DNA. The junction is present only in the assembly; the reads from the assembled individual are not publicly available (see above).

transfer_caveats: The reads are from other individuals. A junction present only in the assembled individual could not be detected, and the kleptoplasts of that individual could not be identified.
In the public assembly, 35% of the bases are N. Sequence in the masked regions could not be searched, at either the DNA or the protein level.

Short reads from animals that contain large amounts of chloroplast DNA cannot reveal an insertion that is present in only a few cells. Library preparation itself joins chloroplast DNA to nuclear DNA, and a genuine insertion in a single cell would add only one molecule to this background.

The analysis of the reads detects plastid DNA that resembles a reference sequence in the panel. Much of the plastid DNA from the less abundant algae in these animals matches the panel with only about 90% identity.
elysia-leucolegnote.locus_text: The start of JBQKML010000381.1 was tested with all reads from the two other individuals, not only those that resemble a reference sequence. The plastid part of the sequence consists of the first 863 bases, which comprise the end of chlL and the first half of chlN. It is followed by 35 bases, a region that was masked by the submitters, and a repetitive element of the slug genome. A read that spans base 863 supports the junction between the plastid DNA and the sequence that follows it in the assembly. A read whose alignment ends at that position continues from the plastid DNA into different sequence.
locus_after: No read spans the junction. The reads whose alignment ends at base 863 continue with the same sequence in both individuals, and this sequence continues chlN in its reading frame; it is the remainder of the gene, as in any plastid genome. Read pairs link both ends of the 863-base region to further plastid DNA.

The plastid sequence has a read depth of about {locus1_depth}× in the Shenzhen individual and {hainan_locus1_depth}× in the Hainan individual, compared with about {slug_depth}× and {hainan_slug_depth}× for the slug nuclear genome. DNA at this abundance is plastid DNA from the food of the animals, not part of the slug genome.

In the two other individuals, therefore, this sequence is ordinary plastid DNA from an alga on which they had fed. In the assembly it lies at the very end of a sequence, and it is joined to nuclear DNA at a position within a gene at which the reads from the other individuals continue with the gene. This is the result expected when an assembler has extended a contig along a single molecule in which plastid DNA is joined to nuclear DNA, as in E. crispata. Whether that molecule formed during library preparation or derived from a cell of the animal cannot be determined, because the reads from the assembled individual are not publicly available. The junction should therefore not be regarded as a feature of the genome of this species.
klepto_rhythm: The closest reference for mapping kleptoplast transcripts is NC_039521.1 (Boodleopsis sp., 75,962 bp, annotated in GenBank), which is 97 to 99% identical to the main plastid type in the two individuals analysed. The plastid contigs from both individuals are available in the downloads.

Transcripts from the other algae present in these animals will map poorly, or not at all, to this reference. A proportion of unmapped plastid-like reads is therefore to be expected, and should not be regarded as noise.

place_notes.JBQKML010000169.1:77000: This locus comprises the ribosomal RNA genes of one of the bacterial sequences in the assembly (see below). The mates match plastid ribosomal RNA genes because the bacterial and plastid genes are related. The bacterium was also present in this individual.
place_notes.JBQKML010000169.1:78000: This locus comprises the ribosomal RNA genes of one of the bacterial sequences in the assembly (see below). The mates match plastid ribosomal RNA genes because the bacterial and plastid genes are related.
place_notes.JBQKML010000169.1:79000: The same ribosomal RNA genes of the bacterial sequence.
place_notes.JBQKML010000169.1:80000: The same ribosomal RNA genes of the bacterial sequence.
place_notes.JBQKML010000169.1:81000: The same ribosomal RNA genes of the bacterial sequence.

break_notes.CM127901.1:11338221: This position is a gap in the assembly (67 bases of N). The reads continue into a transfer RNA gene of the slug that is missing from the assembly at this position; transfer RNA genes are similar in slugs and plastids.

elysia-chlorotica.klepto_lede: E. chlorotica is the best-known example of kleptoplasty: it feeds on the yellow-green alga Vaucheria litorea and retains its chloroplasts for months. Three read sets were analysed, from two adults and from eggs.
klepto_answer: The kleptoplasts in both adults came from Vaucheria litorea. Of the plastid DNA, {donor1_pct} in the long reads and {adult_donor1_pct} in the short reads matches the V. litorea plastid genome. The barcode gene rbcL, extracted from plastid contigs assembled from the short reads, is {adult_rbcL_best_id} identical to V. litorea records over {adult_rbcL_best_len} bases.

The plastid content is high. Plastid DNA makes up {cp_pct} of the sequenced bases in one adult and {adult_cp_pct} in the other, which corresponds to about {depth_ratio} and {adult_depth_ratio} copies of the plastid genome per copy of the slug nuclear genome.

The eggs contain almost no plastid DNA. In {eggs_bases} of egg DNA, only {eggs_cp_reads} read pairs match a plastid sequence of any kind, and two single reads match Vaucheria. Because eggs contain no ingested algal material, this library represents the germline alone. It shows what is inherited, but provides no information about events in the somatic cells of adults (see the gene-transfer page).
klepto_which: Reads and read pairs were assigned to the plastid reference that they match best. The long reads from this species are older, error-prone PacBio RS reads with an accuracy of about 92%, so their identity to the reference reflects the error rate of the reads and not the divergence of the alga. The short reads match with 100% identity.

The plastid read pairs from the short-read library were assembled into contigs with a total length of {adult_contig_kb} kb ({adult_contigs} contigs), compared with 115 kb for the published plastid genome.
klepto_nuclei: The panel contains one nuclear ribosomal DNA record of V. litorea that includes a variable spacer region. No long read matches it. Short reads cannot resolve this question, because they match algal ribosomal DNA records only in the conserved regions that are shared with the slug’s own genes.
klepto_caveats: The two adults are different individuals: a wild-caught animal (isolate EC2010, Martha’s Vineyard) for the long reads and an animal from a laboratory culture for the short reads. Their plastid contents differ ({cp_pct} and {adult_cp_pct} of the bases, respectively).

All six paired-end libraries from the second adult were analysed ({adult_bases}). Because so much of this DNA is chloroplast DNA, only one in 50 of the matching pairs was analysed in detail, and the plastid contigs were assembled from these pairs.
Both runs of the egg library were analysed ({eggs_bases}).
elysia-chlorotica.transfer_lede: The hypothesis that algal genes have been transferred to a slug genome was first proposed for E. chlorotica (Rumpho et al. 2008), and sequencing of egg DNA later found no evidence for it (Bhattacharya et al. 2013). The assembly and three read sets, from two adults and from eggs, were analysed in the same way as for the other species. All reads in the three sets were analysed.
transfer_answer: There is no algal DNA in the germline. In the somatic DNA of one adult there are molecules of the kind expected from insertions, but with these data they cannot be distinguished from chimeras formed during library preparation.

Germline. Egg DNA contains almost no chloroplast DNA ({eggs_cp_reads} read pairs in {eggs_bases}), and none of the fragments of chloroplast DNA in the assembly is present in it. The same reads do contain a fragment of mitochondrial DNA inserted in a chromosome, which is found in two independent molecules, so an inherited insertion of organelle DNA can be detected in this library. None of the Vaucheria nuclear genes previously reported in the slug (psbO, prk, the light-harvesting genes, chlD, chlG and chlH) matches any sequence in the assembly.

Somatic cells. Among the long reads from one adult, {ins_cp} molecules contain a segment of chloroplast DNA flanked on both sides by nuclear DNA. Each is the only such molecule at its locus, and other reads span the locus without the insert. This is the result expected for insertions in single cells. However, {mirror} molecules have the reciprocal structure, nuclear DNA flanked by chloroplast DNA, which cannot result from an insertion into a chromosome, and unrelated nuclear sequences are joined in {bg_rate} of the long reads of this library. The library therefore produces molecules of this kind, and the {ins_cp} cannot be distinguished from them.

No junction is found in two independent molecules. One pair of molecules comes close. The junction that is present in the assembly at the start of RQTK01001031.1, between chloroplast DNA and a satellite repeat of the slug, is supported by a single long read, and a second molecule joins the same region of chloroplast DNA to the same repeat 47 bases away. Neither junction is present in the egg reads, so neither is inherited.

Assembly. The assembly contains {whole_n} small sequences ({whole_bp} bp in total) that consist entirely of Vaucheria plastid DNA, two longer sequences that each contain a region of plastid DNA, and four that contain regions of the slug’s own mitochondrial genome. The protein search also identified {bact_n} bacterial sequences with a total length of {bact_kb} kb.
transfer_assembly: The five small sequences are 94 to 98% identical to the published V. litorea plastid genome over their whole length. They are kleptoplast DNA that was assembled separately and was not removed from the assembly.

loci_readings.RQTK01001031.1:3: The first 1.6 kb of this 174 kb sequence is Vaucheria plastid DNA, comprising most of rpoB and the end of rpoC1, joined to a satellite repeat of the slug. The junction is supported by one long read (see below).
loci_readings.RQTK01001326.1:53256: A 230 bp region of rpoC1 within a 111 kb sequence. No read of any type spans either boundary, and two long reads span the locus without the region.
loci_readings.RQTK01001610.1:44383: A ribosomal RNA gene of bacterial type; the protein search found bacterial genes on other sequences in this assembly.

elysia-chlorotica.numt_text: Four regions of 0.5 to 1.2 kb within nuclear sequences are 99% identical to the slug’s own mitochondrial genome. Nuclear copies of mitochondrial DNA occur in many animals, so these regions were tested with reads in the same way as the plastid regions (see the table below).
reads_main: Frequencies. When all reads of 2 kb or longer are counted in the same way, {join_cp_rate} of the reads containing chloroplast DNA and {join_mt_rate} of the reads containing mitochondrial DNA are joined to nuclear DNA, and {bg_rate} of the nuclear reads are joined to an unrelated nuclear segment. A further {bg_fold_rate} of nuclear reads fold back and continue along their own sequence in the reverse direction. This older library thus contains many chimeric and fold-back molecules, and it joins chloroplast DNA to nuclear DNA at the same frequency as it joins any two sequences. At this frequency, about a hundred reads with a genuine junction would go undetected.

Read structure. {Ins_cp} reads contain a segment of chloroplast DNA, 160 to 1,700 bases long, flanked on both sides by nuclear DNA that is contiguous in the assembly. Each is a single molecule at a different locus, and at all but two of these loci three or four other long reads span the locus without the insert. In two of the reads the nuclear sequence is uninterrupted, and the chloroplast segment is simply additional sequence. This is the result expected for an insertion in a single cell. However, such insertions could have been detected only if they were frequent, because the reads that are long enough to show them cover each position in the genome less than three times.

Evidence that such reads can be library artefacts. Two reads, identified by the same procedure, have the reciprocal structure: a segment of nuclear DNA from a unique position, flanked on both sides by chloroplast DNA that is contiguous in the plastid genome. Insertion of chloroplast DNA into a chromosome cannot produce this structure, whereas a process that transfers a segment of one molecule into another can, and would produce both structures at the same frequency. The two structures are equally frequent, as far as a comparison of two reads with four reads of similar insert size can show. Read SRR7647856.5712567 passes through its chloroplast segment, folds back, and covers the same region of nuclear DNA a second time, and in the second pass the nuclear sequence is uninterrupted at the position of the junction. The chloroplast segment is therefore present on only one strand of that molecule, which is not consistent with chromosomal DNA. Read SRR7647856.1389423 contains a short chloroplast segment within nuclear DNA and then ends in further chloroplast DNA from the same 1,200 bases of the plastid genome, in both orientations.

What cannot be concluded. None of these observations shows that the other reads are library artefacts. With reads of this error rate, and a library with this frequency of chimeras, a molecule from a cell with an insertion cannot be distinguished from a molecule formed during library preparation. Two reads contain a segment of mitochondrial DNA flanked by nuclear DNA in the same way. Nuclear copies of mitochondrial DNA occur in animals, so these two may be genuine, but they also cannot be distinguished from library artefacts. These molecules cannot be re-examined, because an insertion in a single somatic cell of this animal exists nowhere else. PacBio HiFi reads from an adult would show whether molecules with this structure are present. The HiFi libraries on this site, from four other species, contain none.

Recurrent junctions. The reads with a single junction were compared with each other at base level, so that junctions in repetitive DNA would also be detected. A total of {rec_groups} junctions are found in more than one read, and in every case the reads are from the same ZMW, that is, they are multiple passes over a single molecule. No junction is shared by two molecules.

Two pairs of molecules have junctions that are close together, both in the 358-base satellite repeat that makes up about 1% of the slug genome. In {rep_cp} molecules, chloroplast DNA is joined to this satellite. In one pair, the junctions are 40 bases apart in the plastid genome (positions 78,759 and 78,799) and at different positions in the repeat. Among {rep_cp} junctions, about {rep_expected} pairs this close together are expected by chance, so this pair is not significant.

The other pair is at the junction that is present in the assembly, at the start of RQTK01001031.1. Read SRR7647856.731470 contains that junction. In a second molecule, which was sequenced twice (SRR7647856.279702 and .279703, which agree), the chloroplast DNA begins 34 bases further along the plastid genome and the repeat ends 13 bases earlier, so this molecule has a different junction, 47 bases away. In both molecules the chloroplast DNA then extends for about 1.5 kb to the end of the molecule, and the two ends are within 100 bases of each other. Two unrelated events would be this close together in about one in fifty libraries of this kind, so the proximity may be due to chance, but it is more likely that the two molecules are related. The amplified library of E. crispata contains three similar cases, in which chloroplast DNA is joined to a simple repeat of the slug at positions a few bases apart in two molecules. In that library the probable cause is a polymerase that stalls in the repeat and then continues on another molecule. The archive record does not state how the E. chlorotica library was prepared, and there is no other indication of amplification: among {copies_placed} nuclear reads, {copies_pairs} pairs from different ZMWs share both ends to within 30 bases, and {copies_next} pairs share one end and differ at the other by 30 to 60 bases, as expected by chance. Two adjacent insertions in related cells would give the same result. The reads cannot distinguish between these explanations, and the short reads from the other animals provide no further information (see below).
reads_adult: All six paired-end libraries from this adult were analysed ({adult_bases} in total). This animal contained a large amount of chloroplast DNA, which makes up {adult_cp_pct} of the bases.

Frequencies. The mate is in nuclear DNA for {adult_cp_rate} of chloroplast pairs and {adult_slugmt_rate} of mitochondrial pairs. The second value is based on {adult_slugmt_chim_examined} pairs, which is too few to distinguish the two frequencies. In the two libraries from E. leucolegnote there is a similar excess for chloroplast DNA, and the reads from those libraries show why it cannot be interpreted as evidence of insertions. In the random sample, {adult_bg_rate} of nuclear pairs have their two reads on unrelated sequences (the assembly consists of scaffolds, which increases this value). A single read spans a junction in {adult_split_cp_rate} of chloroplast pairs. In absolute numbers, the library contains about {adult_cp_chim_about} pairs that join chloroplast DNA to nuclear DNA. An insertion in a single cell would add one.

Recurrent junctions. Among the pairs analysed, no locus in the slug genome has a cluster of such pairs, no breakpoint is spanned by reads from two molecules, and no two independent molecules have the same junction.

The loci of the long reads with an insertion-like structure. This is a different animal, so an insertion in a somatic cell of the first adult is not expected to be present. The test shows only whether any of these loci contains chloroplast DNA in all animals. The reads from this adult span each of the nine loci {adult_cand_cross} times with uninterrupted nuclear sequence, and no read extends from any of them into chloroplast DNA. Within 1 kb of the loci, {adult_cand_joins_any} pair has its mate in chloroplast DNA, in a part of the plastid genome 12 and 50 kb away from the two segments in the corresponding long read. At the frequency given above, about {adult_cand_expected} such pairs are expected near nine loci by chance.

The junctions with the satellite. The library was searched for reads that leave the plastid genome at the same positions as the long reads and continue into the satellite. None was found, either at these positions or at control positions around them. Only the one in 50 chloroplast pairs that was analysed could be searched, so a junction present in every cell of this animal could have been missed.
reads_eggs: Egg DNA represents the germline only. Eggs contain no chloroplasts, so no chloroplast DNA could have been integrated in them, and events in the somatic cells of adults cannot be detected in this library. Both runs were analysed in full.

Only {eggs_cp_reads} pairs match a plastid genome of any kind; these include two single reads that match Vaucheria. No pair and no read joins chloroplast DNA to nuclear DNA. Mitochondrial DNA makes up {eggs_mt_pct} of the bases. One of {eggs_slugmt_n} mitochondrial pairs has its mate in nuclear DNA, and this pair is not a library artefact (see below). In the libraries from the second adult, about one mitochondrial pair in a thousand is joined to nuclear DNA.

An inherited insertion as a positive control. This pair and a second, independent molecule contain the same structure: 88 bases of mitochondrial DNA (positions 6,201 to 6,288 of the mitochondrial genome) inserted between two adjacent bases of the nuclear sequence RQTK01000018.1, at position 1,186,043. Each molecule extends from nuclear DNA through the whole insert and into the nuclear DNA that follows. The assembly is continuous at this position and lacks the insert. Some of these eggs therefore carry a fragment of mitochondrial DNA in a chromosome, that is, a recent nuclear copy of mitochondrial DNA of the kind known from many animals. It was detected by the test for recurrent junctions, which would have detected an inherited fragment of chloroplast DNA in the same way.

The egg reads span the loci of the nine long reads with an insertion-like structure {eggs_cand_cross} times with uninterrupted nuclear sequence, and none of them joins one of these loci to chloroplast DNA. No read extends from the plastid genome into the satellite. Thus none of the candidates, and neither of the junctions with the satellite, is inherited. This was expected, and does not affect their interpretation as possible events in somatic cells.
elysia-chlorotica.locus_text: For every organelle region within an assembly sequence, reads were aligned to the region together with 3 kb of flanking sequence on each side. At each boundary, a read that spans the boundary supports the junction between the region and its flank. A read whose alignment ends at the boundary continues into different sequence: organelle reads continue as organelle DNA, and reads from the flank continue as other nuclear DNA.
locus_after: The plastid region at the start of RQTK01001031.1. One long read contains the junction as it appears in the assembly, and a second molecule has a different junction 47 bases away (see above). The {locus1_right_stop_in} long reads that reach the boundary from within the region are reads of the plastid genome, which continues at that position; they provide no information about the junction. No short read from the second adult or from the eggs spans it. For the second adult this is not informative, because the assembly at this position was built from a few error-prone reads and is only 94% accurate, and only one chloroplast pair in 50 was analysed. The eggs are decisive for the germline. If these 1.6 kb were inherited, 70 to 150 egg reads would be plastid DNA from this region, whereas the whole egg library contains only {eggs_cp_reads} pairs that match any plastid genome.

The 230 bases of rpoC1 in RQTK01001326.1. No read from any library spans either boundary. Plastid reads cover the region and continue as plastid DNA. Reads that approach from the nuclear side end at its boundaries ({eggs_locus2_left_stop_out} and {eggs_locus2_right_stop_out} reads in the eggs) and continue with nuclear sequence that is absent from the assembly at this position, which on one side consists of additional copies of a 33-base repeat. Two long reads from the first adult span the locus; they lack the region and the adjacent 270 bases. The region is not present in any of the three read sets. It appears to be an artefact introduced by the assembler at a repeat that could not be resolved.

The four mitochondrial regions. Mitochondrial reads cover these regions at a depth of several hundred and continue as mitochondrial DNA. No short read from the second adult or from the eggs spans any of the eight boundaries, whereas a copy present in every cell of the second adult would be spanned about forty times at each boundary. Reads from the flanking sequence end at the boundaries of the regions in RQTK01000434.1 and RQTK01000515.1 (2 to 32 reads per boundary in the second adult and 2 to 4 in the eggs). In RQTK01000432.1, the nuclear sequence that precedes the region occurs a second time 1.8 kb further on, and at that second copy every read that extends beyond its end continues into nuclear DNA. The region in RQTK01002715.1 lies between two repeats that occur at about 60 loci in the assembly, and hundreds of reads from these repeats end at its boundaries. None of the four regions is therefore a nuclear copy of mitochondrial DNA that is present in the second adult or in the eggs. Among the long reads from the first adult, one molecule, which was sequenced twice, spans one boundary of the region in RQTK01000432.1, and one molecule crosses a boundary of the region in RQTK01002715.1 with 82 bases missing. This leaves the same two interpretations as for the chloroplast junctions: either a mitochondrial read that the assembler incorporated into a nuclear sequence, as it did with plastid reads, or a junction present in some cells of that animal.

The 86 bases in RQTK01000372.1 are 92% identical to a spacer region of the plastid genome. Reads from the second adult match them exactly and continue as plastid DNA on both sides, which shows that the alga on which that adult had fed differs from the reference in this region. The reads that span the right boundary ({adult_locus7_right_through} from the second adult and {eggs_locus7_right_through} from the eggs) all start in the run of cytosines at the end of the region and contain none of the part that is recognisable as plastid DNA. No long read covers the locus.
transfer_proteins: The six loci on plastid sequences lie on the plastid fragments described above. The loci of bacterial type lie on fourteen sequences of 18 to 76 kb. When translated in full, each of these sequences is bacterial along its whole length, with {bact_genes} protein-coding regions of bacterial type in {bact_kb} kb and a G+C content of 30 to 35%, compared with {genome_gc} for the genome. For twelve of the fourteen sequences, the most similar proteins are those of Francisella, typically with about 50% identity. The sequences therefore derive from a bacterium related to that genus, which lived in or on the animal and was assembled together with its genome. They are not of algal origin.

One locus has an algal protein as its best match: a cysA gene on RQTK01001990.1. It lies among bacterial genes on one of the fourteen sequences, and the transporter that it encodes occurs in both bacteria and plastids. {Bact_listed} of the loci of bacterial type are included in the gene set published with the assembly, where they are annotated as slug genes.

The search included all 74 Vaucheria litorea proteins in UniProt, among them the nuclear-encoded photosynthesis proteins named in the early reports. The Vaucheria PsbO, phosphoribulokinase, light-harvesting proteins, magnesium chelatase subunits and chlorophyll synthase do not align anywhere in the assembly. Most of the weak alignments mentioned above derive from two long Chlamydomonas proteins that are rich in low-complexity sequence, one annotated as a light-harvesting protein and the other as a magnesium chelatase. These proteins align to low-complexity regions, and the translations of those regions match no known protein. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase matches one locus, which is the slug’s own gene for this enzyme.

protein_readings.RQTK01001031.1: The 1.6 kb plastid region at the start of this sequence (rpoB).

transfer_caveats: The long reads are error-prone, and the reads that are long enough to show an insertion cover each position in the genome less than three times, which is equivalent to the DNA of about one cell. Only insertions present in most cells could have been detected.
The two adults and the eggs are from different animals. An insertion in the somatic cells of one animal cannot be searched for in another.

A gene without a homologue among the 471 query proteins would not be detected by the protein search, and sequence in parts of the genome that are missing from the assembly would not be detected by either search of the assembly. The bacterial sequences listed are those in which the search happened to find a match; the assembly may contain others.
These analyses do not address the possible transfer of RNA or protein from the alga to the slug without integration of DNA into the genome.
klepto_rhythm: Kleptoplast transcripts should be mapped to NC_011600.1, the plastid genome of Vaucheria litorea (115,341 bp, annotated). The short reads from the second adult match it with 100% identity.

When the slug assembly is used as a reference, the plastid fragments and bacterial sequences should be excluded (they are listed on the gene-transfer page). Otherwise, plastid transcripts will map to them and will appear to be transcripts of slug genes.
